title: Indian Missions on Long Island
summary: A short overview of Indian mission activity on Long Island, including missionaries, Native communities, and Christian mission records.
content:
Introduction

History

1672

Besides the members of the Sylvester family, the Manhansets also interacted with numerous Quaker visitors, including John Jay, William Edmundson, and George Fox, founder of the Society of Friends.

George Fox arrived on Shelter Island after a three-day voyage from Rhode Island and led a meeting with the Indigenous inhabitants the following day.

Through a Native American interpreter, Fox led a two-hour preaching service to approximately one hundred Manhansets, including the King and his council during his first week on the island.

The Manhansets were described as sitting “down like Friends”1 and confessed that he spoke the truth. The following Sunday, Fox again guided a large gathering for the Manhansets, which may have possibly included the African residents of Shelter Island.

Before Fox’s departure, meetings were arranged with the Manhansets for every two weeks and Joshua Sylvester, Nathaniel Sylvester’s brother, was scheduled to read Scriptures to them.2

1740

The first missionary in the 1740s was Azariah Horton of Southold and a graduate of Yale, who was not very successful. He recommended a successor; this was Samson Occom, a Mohegan who came first as a teacher, then was ordained in the Presbyterian Church after tutelage by the Rev. Samuel Buell. Remaining as handwriting for 200 years, Occum's diary was published by Dartmouth College and later researched and published by Dr. Gaynell Stone in her History and Archaeology of the Montauk volume.3

1741

Rev. Azariah Horton’s first service to the Rockaway Indians – in the years to come Rev. Horton visits dozens of native communities all over Long Island who gathered in certain areas to hear him preach.4

Rev. Azariah Horton’s visit to Sebonac settlement to preach to Shinnecock Indians.4

1749

Rev. Azariah Horton recommends Samson Occum as his successor.4

1759

Mohegan Indian Rev. Samson Occum, Azariah Horton’s successor, is mentored by Rev. Samuel Buell in East Hampton and is ordained at East Hampton, Aug. 29, 1759 by Suffolk Presbytery. He has already taken over preaching and teaching Horton’s former congregations at Montauk, Shinnecock and Poosepatuck.4

1774 – 1801 (ca.)

Rev. Elisha Paine, Congregationalist, of Hayground, ordains Shinnecock Indian, Peter John. Rev.

Peter John takes over from Mohegan Rev. Samson Occum and visits Indian congregations in Shinnecock, Poosepatuck, Islip and Wading River.5

Azariah Horton in Hunter's account

Hunter summarized Azariah Horton's mission work among Shinnecock and other Long Island Native communities beginning in 1741 and reproduced a July 22, 1741 diary passage from Shinnecock. Mission records must be read critically: they preserve evidence of Native communities and relationships while expressing a missionary's goals and colonial-era judgments. Native people engaged, adapted, challenged, and later led Christian institutions on their own terms.1

Thomas and Lula Ogburn

Hunter remembered the Rev. Thomas Clay Ogburn arriving at Shinnecock in October 1910 with his wife, Lula Campbell Ogburn. She connected their work with the Shinnecock church, education, and relationships extending into Southampton's Black and Native church communities. Hunter recorded Lula Ogburn's appointment to the reservation school in 1914 and presented their long service as part of Shinnecock community history.2

Questions visitors ask

Open a question for a concise answer, context, and sources.

How did missions and colonial schooling affect Native communities on Long Island?

Missions and colonial schooling pressured Native communities to assimilate, suppressing Algonquian languages. However, communities adapted Christianity and English literacy as powerful tools of resilience, using written English to petition for land rights and establishing independent Native-led churches that still serve as cultural anchors today.

Missions and colonial schooling on Long Island represented intense assimilation pressures, yet Native communities strategically adapted these institutions to preserve their social cohesion and defend their sovereignty. In the mid-eighteenth century, Mohegan minister Samson Occom served as a schoolmaster at Montauk, teaching English literacy while respecting Native customs, as documented in 'The Collected Writings of Samson Occom' and 'Samson Occum - A Montauk Schoolmaster'. Later, Shinnecock preacher Rev. Paul Cuffee led independent, Native-focused congregations. While the primary goal of white missionary societies was cultural assimilation and the eradication of Indigenous languages, Long Island nations transformed churches, such as the Shinnecock Presbyterian Church and the Poospatuck temple, into vital community sanctuaries and political meeting places. Literacy in English became a crucial defensive weapon, enabling leaders to write petitions, audit colonial deeds, and challenge illegal land grabs in New York courts. Rather than indicating a total loss of Indigenous identity, adopting Christian practices and English literacy represented a highly sophisticated strategy of survival and adaptation, allowing families to protect their ancestral kinship networks while navigating a hostile colonial legal landscape.
